definition: likelihood principle is the proposition that, given a [statistical model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model), all the evidence in a [sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_(statistics)) relevant to model parameters is contained in the [likelihood function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Likelihood_function).

likelihood-ratio test is a [hypothesis test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothesis_test) that involves comparing the [goodness of fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodness_of_fit) of two competing [statistical model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model)s, typically one found by [maximization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_optimization) over the entire [parameter space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameter_space) and another found after imposing some [constraint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constraint_(mathematics)), based on the ratio of their [likelihoods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Likelihood_function).

Likelihoodist statistics or likelihoodism is an approach to [statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics) that exclusively or primarily uses the [likelihood function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Likelihood_function).

definition: Lindley's paradox is a [counterintuitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterintuitive) situation in [statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics) in which the [Bayesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_inference) and [frequentist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequentist) approaches to a [hypothesis testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothesis_testing) problem give different results for certain choices of the [prior distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prior_distribution).
Line fitting is the process of constructing a [straight line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_line) that has the best fit to a series of data points.

Linear least squares (LLS) is the [least squares approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least_squares_approximation) of [linear functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_functions) to data.
linear model refers to any model which assumes [linearity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linearity) in the system.

Linear prediction is a mathematical operation where future values of a [discrete-time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_time_and_continuous_time) [signal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_processing) are estimated as a [linear function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_transformation) of previous samples.

linear predictor function is a [linear function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_function) ([linear combination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_combination)) of a set of coefficients and explanatory variables ([independent variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_variable)s), whose value is used to predict the outcome of a [dependent variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependent_variable).

linear regression is a [model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model) that estimates the relationship between a [scalar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalar_(mathematics)) response ([dependent variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependent_variable)) and one or more explanatory variables (regressor or [independent variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_variable)).
Linear trend estimation is a [statistical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics) technique used to analyze [data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data) patterns.
Linguistic demography is the [statistical study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics) of [language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language)s among all populations.

LIONsolver is an integrated software for [data mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_mining), [business intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_intelligence), [analytics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytics), and [modeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modeling_and_simulation) and [reactive business intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_business_intelligence) approach.

Liouville's theorem, named after the French mathematician [Joseph Liouville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Liouville), is a key theorem in classical [statistical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_mechanics) and [Hamiltonian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_mechanics).

definition: putout (PO) is awarded to a defensive player who (generally while in secure possession of the ball) records an [out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_(baseball)) by one of the following methods: * [Tagging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tag_play) a runner with the ball when the runner is not touching a base (a [tagout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tag_out)) * Catching a batted ball on the fly (a [flyout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flyout)) * Retrieving a batted ball hit along the ground which a defensive player subsequently throws to another defensive player who then catches it- the latter simultaneously occupying a base, or by subsequently touching a base while in possession of the ball- thus recording an out of a batter or runner, before the batter, or non-batting runner, can touch the base to which he is compelled to advance (a [force out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force_play)- referred to as a [groundout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ground_out_(baseball)) if the player who has been put out is the [batter-runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batter-runner) attempting to reach first base- or, if done after a flyout, a [doubling off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubling_off)).

sampling distribution or finite-sample distribution is the [probability distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution) of a given [random-sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_sample)-based [statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistic).

sampling errors are incurred when the statistical characteristics of a [population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_population) are estimated from a subset, or [sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sample_(statistics)), of that population.

sampling fraction is the ratio of [sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sample_(statistics)) size to [population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_population) size or, in the context of [stratified sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratified_sampling), the ratio of the sample size to the size of the stratum.

sampling probability (also known as inclusion probability) of an [element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Element_(statistics)) or member of the population, is its [probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability) of becoming part of the sample during the drawing of a single sample.

definition: Statistical conclusion validity is the degree to which conclusions about the relationship among [variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_(research)) based on the data are correct or This is because [correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation)s are attenuated (weakened) by reduced variability (see, for example, the equation for the [Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_product-moment_correlation_coefficient) which uses score variance in its estimation).

Statistical graphics, also known as statistical graphical techniques, are [graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics) used in the field of [statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics) for [data visualization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_visualization).

Statistical inference is the process of using [data analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_analysis) to infer properties of an underlying [probability distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution).

Statistical learning theory is a framework for [machine learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning) drawing from the fields of [statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics) and [functional analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_analysis).

Statistical machine translation (SMT) is a [machine translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_translation) approach where translations are generated on the basis of [statistical model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model)s whose parameters are derived from the analysis of bilingual [text corpora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text_corpora).

statistical mechanics is a mathematical framework that applies [statistical methods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics) and [probability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_theory) to large assemblies of microscopic entities.

statistical model is a [mathematical model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_model) that embodies a set of [statistical assumptions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_assumptions) concerning the generation of [sample data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sample_(statistics)) (and similar data from a larger [population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_population)).

model specification is part of the process of building a [statistical model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model): specification consists of selecting an appropriate [functional form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) for the model and choosing which variables to include.
model validation is the task of evaluating whether a chosen [statistical model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model) is appropriate or not.

Statistical Modelling is a bimonthly [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-reviewed) [scientific journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_journal) covering [statistical model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model)ling.

definition: uncertain data is data that contains [noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurement_error) that makes it deviate from the correct, intended or original values.
Uncertainty or incertitude refers to situations involving imperfect or unknown [information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information).
uncertainty coefficient, also called proficiency, entropy coefficient or Theil's U, is a measure of nominal [association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_(statistics)).

Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is the science of quantitative characterization and estimation of [uncertainties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty) in both computational and real world applications.

Uncomfortable science, as identified by [statistician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistician) [John Tukey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tukey), comprises situations in which there is a need to draw an [inference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_inference) from a limited [sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sample_(statistics)) of [data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data), where further samples influenced by the same [cause system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cause_system) will not be available.
